We then extend the framework to second-order criticality through $\tau_k = \max\{\|g_k\|, -\lambda_k^-\}$, obtaining convergence to second-order critical points with the worst-case complexity $\mathcal{O}(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-2}\varepsilon_H^{-1}, \varepsilon_H^{-3}\})$, which reduces to $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ for a common tolerance and is sharp for quadratic models. Finally we establish eventual inactivity of the constraint and superlinear convergence, isolating the two properties of the radius rule through which the mechanism enters; the rate itself is mechanism-independent. The criticality-anchored and capped gradient-scaled rules reach inactivity only under a side condition, $\zeta > \overline{\kappa}$ or $\overline{\mu} > \overline{\kappa}$, with $\overline{\kappa}$ a constant of the solution that cannot be checked in advance. These conditions are necessary, not artefacts: on $f(x) = \sin(x)/x$, $\overline{\kappa}$ is unbounded over the minimisers, so no parameter value meets the condition at all of them. Among the rules tied to a criticality measure, only those with an unbounded multiplier escape such a constant.
item.dc:creator: J\'er\'emy Rieussec, Fabian Bastin

item.title: Tight lower bounds for Lipschitz geodesically convex optimization on hyperbolic space
item.description: arXiv:2610.26815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We determine the dimension-independent first-order query complexity of minimizing a Lipschitz geodesically convex (g-convex) function on hyperbolic space. Given a ball of radius $r$ containing a global minimizer, we prove that $\Omega(\zeta_r/\epsilon^2)$ queries are necessary to attain accuracy $\epsilon Mr$, where $M$ is the Lipschitz constant and $\zeta_r=r/\tanh r$ captures the effect of curvature. This matches the known $O(\zeta_r/\epsilon^2)$ upper bound for the Riemannian subgradient method (Zhang and Sra, 2016). This is the first query-complexity result for g-convex optimization that is tight simultaneously in curvature and target accuracy. The standard Euclidean recipe of constructing hard instances as maxima of affine functions does not transfer to hyperbolic space, so the lower bound requires a new mechanism. Our starting point is the worst-function construction of Criscitiello and Boumal (2023, Appendix A). It gives the same lower bound for a subclass of algorithms, including the subgradient method, whose queries remain in prescribed g-convex regions. We retain this geometric setup and carefully tune and augment their hard function to accommodate every deterministic first-order algorithm. The key new mechanism is an advance-or-stall scheme: when a query lies in these regions, the oracle reveals at most one new information direction (advance); when a query leaves them, we show that the oracle can answer without revealing any new hidden direction (stall). Unlike earlier curvature-dependent lower bounds, the proof uses no ball-packing argument.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Criscitiello

item.title: Recovered-Coefficient Discontinuous Galerkin Approximation of an Averaged-State Credit-Rating Migration PDE
item.description: arXiv:2107.09248v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop and analyze a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method for an averaged-state regularization of a credit-rating migration equation, in which the volatility switch is smoothed at scale $\eps$ and evaluated at a mollified state of width $\ell$. The diffusion operator is written in conservative form and discretized by symmetric interior penalty, and the effective drift by upwinding. The nonlinear coefficients are evaluated from a recovered state obtained by Oswald averaging, the model mollifier, and an explicit norm cutoff calibrated by a data-computable maximum bound. The recovered coefficients are single-valued and uniformly $W^{2,\infty}$, so the standard upwind energy identity holds, and the recovery is Lipschitz from $L^2$ and compatible with the projected exact state at order $h^{p+1}$. For fixed $(\eps,\ell)$ we prove well-posedness and a maximum bound for the continuous problem, an $O(\ell^2)$ distance to the pointwise-regularized model, stability of the frozen-coefficient backward Euler DG scheme, and an $O(h^p+\Delta t)$ error estimate in the DG energy norm; an exact Nitsche--lifting identity covers nonhomogeneous Dirichlet data. Under local transversality, the regularized migration boundary is recovered at a proved, suboptimal rate. Computations with the analyzed scheme confirm the predicted rates and report the quantities on which the analysis rests.
item.dc:creator: Davood Damircheli

item.title: Lattice-based kernel approximation and serendipitous weights for parametric PDEs in very high dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2303.17755v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe a fast method for solving elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs) with uncertain coefficients using kernel interpolation at a lattice point set. By representing the input random field of the system using the model proposed by Kaarnioja, Kuo, and Sloan (SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 2020), in which a countable number of independent random variables enter the random field as periodic functions, it was shown by Kaarnioja, Kazashi, Kuo, Nobile, and Sloan (Numer. Math. 2022) that the lattice-based kernel interpolant can be constructed for the PDE solution as a function of the stochastic variables in a highly efficient manner using fast Fourier transform (FFT). In this work, we discuss the connection between our model and the popular "affine and uniform model" studied widely in the literature of uncertainty quantification for PDEs with uncertain coefficients. We also propose a new class of weights entering the construction of the kernel interpolant $-$ serendipitous weights $-$ which dramatically improve the computational performance of the kernel interpolant for PDE problems with uncertain coefficients, and allow us to tackle function approximation problems up to very high dimensionalities. Numerical experiments are presented to showcase the performance of the serendipitous weights.
item.dc:creator: Vesa Kaarnioja, Frances Y. Kuo, Ian H. Sloan

item.title: Generalizing Riemann curvature to Regge metrics
item.description: arXiv:2311.01603v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we propose a generalization of the Riemann curvature tensor on manifolds (of dimension two or higher) endowed with a Regge metric. Specifically, while all components of the metric tensor are assumed to be smooth within elements of a triangulation of the manifold, they need not be smooth across element interfaces, where only continuity of the tangential components is assumed. While linear derivatives of the metric can be generalized to Schwartz distributions, similarly generalizing the classical Riemann curvature tensor, a nonlinear second-order derivative of the metric, requires more care. We propose a generalization that combines the classical angle defect and jumps in the second fundamental form across element interfaces and argue its correctness. Specifically, if a piecewise smooth metric approximates a globally smooth metric, then our generalized Riemann curvature tensor approximates the classical Riemann curvature tensor associated with the latter. Moreover, we show that if the metric approximation converges at some rate in a mesh-dependent norm equivalent to the $L^2$ norm, then the curvature approximation converges in the negative Sobolev space $H^{-2}$, the dual space of $H^2_0$, at the same rate, under additional assumptions. By appropriate contractions of the generalized Riemann curvature tensor, this work also provides generalizations of scalar curvature, the Ricci curvature tensor, and the Einstein tensor in any dimension.
item.dc:creator: Jay Gopalakrishnan, Michael Neunteufel, Joachim Sch\"oberl, Max Wardetzky

item.title: High-dimensional sparse recovery from function samples - Decoders, guarantees and instance optimality
item.description: arXiv:2503.16209v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the reconstruction of multivariate functions from samples using sparse recovery techniques. For Square Root Lasso, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, and Compressive Sampling Matching Pursuit, we demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that they allow us to recover functions from a small number of random samples. In contrast to Basis Pursuit Denoising, the deployed decoders only require a search space $V_J$ spanned by dictionary elements indexed by $J$ and a sparsity parameter $n$ to guarantee an $L_2$-approximation error decaying no worse than a best $n$-term approximation error and the truncation error with respect to the search space $V_J$ and the uniform norm. We show that this happens simultaneously for all admissible functions if the number of samples scales as $n\log^2 n\log |J|$, coming from known bounds for the RIP for matrices built upon bounded orthonormal systems. As a consequence, we obtain bounds for sampling widths in function classes. In addition, we establish lower bounds on the required sample complexity, which show that the log-factor in $\vert J \vert$ is indeed necessary to obtain such {\em instance-optimal} error guarantees. Finally, we conduct several numerical experiments to show that our theoretical bounds are reasonable and compare the discussed decoders in practice.
item.dc:creator: Moritz Moeller, Sebastian Neumayer, Kateryna Pozharska, Tizian Sommerfeld, Tino Ullrich

item.title: Enhanced randomized Douglas-Rachford method for linear systems: Improved probabilities and adaptive momentum
item.description: arXiv:2506.10261v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Randomized iterative methods have gained recent interest in machine learning and signal processing for solving large-scale linear systems. One such example is the randomized Douglas-Rachford (RDR) method, which updates the iterate by reflecting it through two randomly selected hyperplanes and taking a convex combination with the current point. In this work, we enhance RDR by introducing improved sampling strategies and an adaptive heavy-ball momentum scheme. Specifically, we incorporate without-replacement sampling and volume sampling into RDR and establish linear convergence in expectation for both schemes. For without-replacement sampling, we further establish a larger one-step descent than that of conventional RDR. For volume sampling, the convergence rate explicitly incorporates geometric information, and a tighter comparison with RDR is obtained under additional structural assumptions. Furthermore, we develop an adaptive momentum mechanism that determines the relaxation and momentum parameters directly from the iteration information without manual tuning. We establish linear convergence in expectation for the resulting method. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods across a range of problem settings.
item.dc:creator: Liqi Guo, Ruike Xiang, Deren Han, Jiaxin Xie

item.title: On maximal curves of $n$-correct sets
item.description: arXiv:2507.11207v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ is an $n$-correct set of nodes in the plane, that is, it admits a unisolvent interpolation with bivariate polynomials of total degree less than or equal to $n.$ Then an algebraic curve $q$ of degree $k\le n$ can pass through at most $d(n,k):={{n+2}\choose {2}}-{{n+2-k}\choose {2}}$ nodes of $\mathcal{X}$. A curve $q$ of degree $k\le n$ is called maximal if it passes through exactly $d(n,k)$ nodes of $\mathcal{X}$. In particular, a maximal line is a line passing through $d(n,1)=n+1$ nodes of $\mathcal{X}$. Maximal curves are an important tool for the study of $n$-correct sets. We present new properties of maximal curves, as well as extensions of known properties.
item.dc:creator: H. Hakopian, G. Vardanyan, N. Vardanyan

item.title: DDFEM: A Python Package for Diffuse Domain Methods
item.description: arXiv:2507.16964v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) on complex domains can present significant computational challenges. The Diffuse Domain Method (DDM) is an alternative that reformulates the partial differential equations on a larger, simpler domain. The original geometry is embedded into the problem by representing it with a phase-field function. This paper introduces DDFEM, an extensible Python package to provide a framework for transforming PDEs into a Diffuse Domain formulation. We aim to make the application of a variety of different Diffuse Domain approaches more accessible and straightforward to use. The DDFEM package includes features to intuitively define complex domains by combining signed distance functions and provides a number of Diffuse Domain transformers for general second-order evolution equations. In addition, we present a new approach for combining multiple boundary conditions of different types on distinct boundary segments. This is achieved by applying a normalised weighting, derived from the component signed distance functions, to combine the additional boundary terms in the Diffuse Domain formulations without requiring additional phase fields. The domain definition and Diffuse Domain transformation provided by our package are designed to be compatible with a wide range of existing finite element solvers without requiring code alterations. Both the original (non-linear) PDEs provided by the user and the resulting transformed PDEs on the extended domain are defined using the Unified Form Language (UFL). Here we focus on the software implementation and demonstrate its effectiveness across a range of problems.
item.dc:creator: Luke Benfield, Andreas Dedner

item.title: On the usage of $2$-node lines in $n$-correct and $GC_n$ sets
item.description: arXiv:2508.13289v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An $n$-correct set $\mathcal{X}$ in the plane is a set of nodes admitting unique interpolation with bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $n$. A $k$-node line is a line passing through exactly $k$ nodes of $\mathcal{X}.$ A line can pass through at most $n+1$ nodes of an $n$-correct set. An $(n+1)$-node line is called maximal line (C. de Boor, 2007). We say that a node $A\in\mathcal{X}$ uses a line $\ell,$ if $\ell$ is a factor of the fundamental polynomial of the node $A.$ Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $n$-correct set. One of the main problems we study in this paper is to determine the maximum possible number of used $2$-node lines that share a common node $B \in\mathcal{X}.$ We show that this number equals $n$. Moreover, if there are $n$ such $2$-node lines, then $\mathcal{X}$ contains exactly $n$ maximal lines not passing through the common node $B$. Furthermore, if $\mathcal{X}$ is $GC_n$ set, there exists an additional maximal line passing through $B$. Hence, in this case, $\mathcal{X}$ has $n+1$ maximal lines and is Carnicer ~ Gasca set of degree $n$. Note that Carnicer ~ Gasca sets of degree $n$ with a prescribed set of $n$ used $2$-node lines can be readily constructed.
item.dc:creator: Hakop Hakopian, Gagik Vardanyan, Navasard Vardanyan

item.title: Diffuse Domain Methods with Dirichlet Boundary Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2509.25115v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The solution of partial differential equations (PDEs) on complex domains often presents a significant computational challenge by requiring the generation of fitted meshes. The Diffuse Domain Method (DDM) is an alternative which reformulates the problem on a larger, simple domain where the complex geometry is represented by a smooth phase-field function.This paper introduces and analyses several new DDM methods for solving problems with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We derive two new methods from the mixed formulation of the governing equations. This approach transforms the essential Dirichlet conditions into natural boundary conditions. Additionally, we develop coercive formulations based on Nitsche's method. We provide proofs of coercivity for all new methods and also for some approximations found in the literature for a wide range of linear advection-diffusion problems.Numerical experiments demonstrate the improved accuracy of the new methods, and reveal the balance between $L^2$ and $H^1$ errors. The practical effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the simulation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on two fluid dynamics benchmark problems.
item.dc:creator: Luke Benfield, Andreas Dedner

item.title: Branched Signature Model
item.description: arXiv:2511.00018v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we introduce the branched signature model, motivated by the branched rough path framework of [Gubinelli, Journal of Differential Equations, 248(4), 2010], which generalizes the classical geometric rough path. We establish a universal approximation theorem for the branched signature model and demonstrate that iterative compositions of lower-level signature maps can approximate higher-level signatures. Furthermore, building on the existence of the extension map proposed in [Hairer-Kelly. Annales de l'Institue Henri Poincar\'e, Probabilit\'es et Statistiques 51, no. 1 (2015)], we show how to explicitly construct the extension of the original paths into higher-dimensional spaces via a map $\Psi$, so that the branched signature can be realized as the classical geometric signature of the extended path. This framework not only provides an efficient computational scheme for branched signatures but also opens new avenues for data-driven modeling and applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through two representative applications: rough volatility calibration and optimal execution.
item.dc:creator: Munawar Ali, Qi Feng

item.title: Smoothing Newton Methods for Evolving Piecewise Smooth Systems Arising from Parabolic PDEs with Hysteresis
item.description: arXiv:2511.22424v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Implicit discretizations of parabolic partial differential equations with hysteresis pose significant challenges for the design of robust nonlinear solvers due to the underlying history dependence. In this work, we derive a unified abstract formulation for the resulting nonlinear systems and show that their nonlinearities possess a monotone piecewise smooth structure with evolving switching behavior. Motivated by this structure, we develop a smoothing Newton method based on structure-preserving smoothing criteria, combining monotonicity preservation with an intermediate slope property. Under these conditions, the proposed method is shown to be globally convergent and locally Q-quadratically convergent. To enable practical implementation, we further introduce an explicit arc-based smoothing construction, thereby bridging the gap between abstract convergence theory and implementable algorithms. Numerical experiments for transient eddy-current problems with Preisach hysteresis demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the proposed method compared with existing approaches.
item.dc:creator: Shu Xu, Liqun Cao

item.title: Numerical analysis of a locking-free primal hybrid method for linear elasticity with $H(\mathrm{div})$-conforming stress recovery
item.description: arXiv:2601.21635v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we study a primal hybrid finite element method for the approximation of linear elasticity problems, posed in terms of displacement, an auxiliary pressure field, and a Lagrange multiplier related to the traction. We develop a general analysis for the existence and uniqueness of the solution for the discrete problem, which is applied to the construction of stable approximation spaces on triangular and quadrilateral meshes. The use of these spaces lead to optimal convergence orders, resulting in a locking-free method capable of providing robust approximations for nearly incompressible problems. Finally, we propose a strategy for recovering the stress field from the hybrid solution by solving element-wise sub-problems. The resulting stress approximation is $H(\mathrm{div})$-conforming, locally equilibrated, weakly symmetric, and robust to locking.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Taraschi, Maicon Ribeiro Correa

item.title: Data Completion for Electrical Impedance Tomography by Conditional Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.07813v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data scarcity is a fundamental barrier in Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT), as undersampled Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) measurements can substantially degrade conductivity reconstructions. We address this bottleneck by completing partially observed DtN measurements using a diffusion based generative model. Specifically, we train a conditional diffusion model to learn the distribution of DtN data and to infer full measurement vectors given partial observations. Our approach supports flexible source receiver configurations and can be used as a plug in preprocessing step with off the shelf EIT solvers. Under mild assumptions on the polygon conductivity class, we derive nonasymptotic end to end bounds on the distributional discrepancy between the completed and ground truth DtN measurements. In numerical experiments, we couple the proposed diffusion completion procedure with a deep learning based inverse solver and compare its performance against the same solver with full measurement data. The results show that diffusion completion enables reconstructions comparable to the full data baseline while using only 1% of the measurements. In contrast, standard baselines such as matrix completion require 30% of the measurements to achieve similar reconstruction quality.
item.dc:creator: Ke Chen, Haizhao Yang, Chugang Yi

item.title: Arbitrary order stationarity preserving stabilized finite elements for multidimensional nonlinear hyperbolic problems. Application to the Euler equations with gravity
item.description: arXiv:2603.23185v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop arbitrarily high-order, stationarity-preserving stabilized finite element methods for multidimensional nonlinear hyperbolic balance laws on Cartesian grids. We aim at approximating all the steady states of the problem at hand, including non-trivial genuinely multidimensional equilibria, with a level of accuracy higher than the nominal one of the underlying scheme. We formalize more precisely the meaning of stationarity preservation, providing some technical conditions for its realizability. We then recast the multidimensional global-flux quadrature of Barsukow et al. (Num. Meth. PDEs, 2025) as a local preprocessing of the physical fluxes that maps continuous polynomial vector fields to a local space with Raviart--Thomas-type structure. Both the Galerkin and SUPG formulations are recast in this setting. The resulting methods extend the stationarity-preserving finite-volume approach of Barsukow et al. (J. Comput. Phys., 2026) to high-order continuous finite elements and Barsukow et al. (Num. Meth. PDEs, 2025) to nonlinear balance laws. We analyze key properties of the proposed schemes, including local conservation and nodal superconvergence of the discrete steady kernel, and we discuss their relation to low-Mach-compliant discretizations. We apply the framework to the compressible Euler equations with gravity. A simple source-term reformulation yields machine-precision preservation of isothermal hydrostatic equilibria. Extensive numerical benchmarks, including moving equilibrium, near-equilibrium, and instability-dominated regimes, demonstrate clear improvements in robustness and accuracy over standard SUPG and reference finite-volume methods.
item.dc:creator: Moussa Ziggaf, Davide Torlo, Mario Ricchiuto

item.title: A second-order energy-stable sequential regularization scheme for the Navier-Stokes equations
item.description: arXiv:2603.26027v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we construct a second-order decoupled scheme for the Navier-Stokes equations based on the idea of the auxiliary variable and the sequential regularization method (SRM). The proposed scheme enjoys unconditional energy stability, which is generally unavailable for the existing SRM, while preserving its key advantage of avoiding artificial pressure boundary conditions and maintaining the original velocity boundary conditions. We establish a viscosity-independent low-order stability estimate and a higher-order stability estimate for the proposed scheme. Furthermore, we derive global-in-time second-order error estimates in two dimensions and corresponding local-in-time estimates in three dimensions, without imposing any time-step restrictions. A series of numerical experiments confirm the convergence and stability, and demonstrate improved accuracy and incompressibility control compared with the projection method and the conventional SRM. In particular, both high-Reynolds-number and three-dimensional numerical simulations further demonstrate the robustness and reliability of the proposed method for complex incompressible flows.
item.dc:creator: Zhaoyang Wang, Ping Lin

item.title: Quasi-random splitting method for accurate and efficient multiphysics simulation
item.description: arXiv:2603.27654v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a quasi-random operator splitting method for evolution equations driven by multiple mechanisms. The method uses a one-dimensional low-discrepancy sequence to determine the ordering of the subflows through a direct point-to-permutation construction, while applying each subflow exactly once per time step. Thus, for a decomposition into \(p\) operators, the proposed method requires only \(p\) subflow evaluations per step, compared with essentially \(2p-2\) evaluations for the classical multi-operator Strang splitting when \(p\geq 3\). In contrast to randomized splitting, the quasi-random ordering is deterministic once the underlying sequence is fixed and avoids the run-to-run fluctuations caused by random permutations. To analyze the resulting scheme, we develop a convergence framework that connects the discrepancy of the induced operator orderings with cancellation of the leading commutator errors accumulated over time. For an arbitrary fixed number of bounded linear operators, we establish a global error of order \(O(\tau^2\log N)\), equivalently \(O(\tau^2|\log\tau|)\) for fixed terminal time, which is essentially second order. We further extend the same cancellation mechanism to the nonlinear Allen--Cahn equation and obtain the same essentially second-order convergence behavior under suitable Sobolev regularity assumptions. Numerical experiments for bounded linear systems and the Allen--Cahn equation confirm the predicted convergence rates and show that the proposed quasi-random splitting strategy retains the low per-step computational cost of a Lie-type splitting method while achieving accuracy close to second order.
item.dc:creator: Lei Li, Yunxiao Liu, Chenchen Wan

item.title: Tree-Adaptive Multiscale Kernel Lasso in Samplet Coordinates
item.description: arXiv:2604.01794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a novel framework for sparse multiscale kernel approximation of large scattered data problems based on a samplet representation. Samplets form a multiresolution analysis of localized discrete signed measures and enable quasi-sparse representations of kernel matrices associated to asymptotically smooth kernels as well as smoothness detection of scattered data. Building on the latter, we introduce an adaptive data site selection strategy based on the native reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm of the samplet expansion coefficients. The selection results in a small set of representative data sites, significantly reducing the effective problem size. On the corresponding reduced kernel subspace, we solve an $\ell^1$-regularized least-squares problem using a trust-region semismooth Newton method in a normal-map formulation, stabilized by an online low-rank SVD on the active set to handle the notorious ill-conditioning of kernel matrices. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, including multi-kernel models with varying lengthscales, demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves accurate reconstructions with considerably sparser representations and good computational efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Sara Avesani, Gaia Fumagalli, Michael Multerer, Chiara Segala

item.title: Galerkin Approximation of the Fractional Sobolev Constant
item.description: arXiv:2605.13347v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish sharp estimates for the discrete optimal constant of the fractional Sobolev inequality in dimension $N\geq 1$, with fractional exponent $s\in (0,\min\{1,N/2\})$. The convergence rates that we establish take place for the Galerkin approximation with piecewise linear elements, when the problem is posed in the unit ball, for which we employ a quasi-uniform and regular mesh. Since the infimum defining the fractional Sobolev constant is not attained on bounded domains, these estimates quantify how far a piecewise affine mesh of size $h$ can resolve the concentration of the optimizers: the discrete minimizers are close to bubbles concentrated at the scale $h^{2(2-s)/(N+4(1-s))}$, and the energy gap is exactly of order $h^{2(2-s)(N-2s)/(N+4(1-s))}$.
item.dc:creator: Andreea Dima, Liviu I. Ignat

item.title: Motion-Enabled Tomography of Gaussian-Mixture Particles under Unknown Rigid-Body Motion with Parabolic Trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2605.18210v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reconstructing objects with unknown position and/or orientation arises in applications spanning geology to cryo-ET. When the relative motion between the object and the sensing apparatus provides sufficient angular coverage, computerized tomography offers a powerful means of reconstruction. For such scenarios, we propose a parametric spatiotemporal model applied to Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), in which each constituent Gaussian is parameterized by its own angular velocity, parabolic trajectory, and morphology. GMM are a suitable means of reconstruction because they (i) admit accurate approximations in object space and (ii) have a closed form expression under the ray transform; enabling efficient forward predictions and analysis in data space. By decoupling the projectile motion from the rotation and morphology, the full optimization problem can be reduced to two lower-dimensional sub-problems that are easier to optimize. The corresponding algorithm --- which is applicable to objects in Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension --- is validated on an extensive set of noisy 2D simulations. Its performance provides promise for further experimentation in more complex scenarios, such as higher dimensions, objects with deformable body mechanics, and on physical datasets.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Burrows, Ozan \"Oktem, Can Evren Yarman

item.title: Computing statistical solutions of a Mach 2000 astrophysical jet
item.description: arXiv:2605.25282v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The multi-dimensional compressible Euler equations admit non-unique entropy solutions in turbulent regimes, and extreme-Mach astrophysical flows are a natural setting in which this breakdown of deterministic well-posedness becomes computationally visible. We compute statistical solutions of a Mach~2000 astrophysical jet, defined as the pushforward of an initial probability measure through a vectorial lattice Boltzmann method, by Monte Carlo sampling with $M=1000$ realizations on grids of up to $12.8$ million cells. Under mesh refinement the individual realizations diverge pathwise, while the statistical solution converges: Wasserstein distances of the one- and two-point marginals, the ensemble mean, and the ensemble standard deviation all exhibit stable positive convergence rates. A spatially resolved analysis along the jet axis traces this dichotomy to the structure of the one-point laws, which are numerically Dirac in the undisturbed core, skewed in the sheared turbulent regions, and intermittent two-state mixtures at the random leading front. We conclude that the computed statistical solution is non-Dirac and remains stable in the extreme compressible regime, in which no strong solution is expected to exist.
item.dc:creator: Stephan Simonis, Gauthier Wissocq

item.title: Bridging Scales: Asymptotic Analysis and AI-Assisted Formalization
item.description: arXiv:2606.10138v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Asymptotic analysis is one of the classical tools for bridging models across scales. Behind many such derivations lies a common symbolic structure: an ansatz, a substitution, an order-by-order matching procedure, and the extraction of effective equations or interface conditions. This article revisits that structure through two representative bridges: the kinetic-to-fluid limit, illustrated by radiative transfer with interface layers and by neural-network approximations of Boltzmann equations, and the quantum-to-classical limit, illustrated by the Frozen Gaussian Approximation and its Dirac extension. We then explain why such derivations are natural candidates for AI-assisted formalization: their recurring symbolic structures can be organized, verified, and reused. In this sense, a carefully structured expository paper may serve not only as a review, but also as a mathematical seed for future AI-assisted environments.
item.dc:creator: Xu Yang

item.title: Bregman-projected mirror methods for regularized stationary mean-field games
item.description: arXiv:2606.19611v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop and analyze a Bregman-projected mirror iteration for low-order regularizations of stationary mean-field game (MFG) systems in their natural Banach space setting. For separable Hamiltonians of the form $H(x,p,m)=H_0(x,p)-g(m)$, with quadratic or super-quadratic Hamiltonian growth and linear or super-linear density couplings, we formulate a low-order $\bar\gamma$-Laplacian regularization of the stationary MFG system as a variational inequality on $L^{\bar\beta}(\mathbb T^d)\times W^{1,\bar\gamma}(\mathbb T^d)$. To approximate solutions of this regularized variational inequality, we introduce a Bregman geometry matched to the mixed Lebesgue-Sobolev exponents of the problem and analyze the exact constrained one-step mirror iteration and a frozen two-step variant. Under quantitative monotonicity of the coupling, both exact iterations converge strongly to the unique solution of the regularized variational inequality for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, under natural summability conditions on the step sizes. Along weakly convergent vanishing-regularization sequences, we also prove strong convergence in the full product space. Numerical experiments in one and two dimensions show first-order accuracy on manufactured solutions and weak dependence of outer iteration counts on the tested grids. At matched effective step sizes, the frozen two-step and one-step implementations agree up to inner-solve accuracy, while the latter requires fewer mirror solves.
item.dc:creator: Hussain Al Abdulaziz, Yuri Ashrafyan, Yeva Gevorgyan, Diogo Gomes

item.title: A multilevel stochastic-gradient neural solver for boundary integral equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.00560v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a multilevel stochastic-gradient neural solver (MLSG) for second-kind boundary integral equations. MLSG represents the unknown boundary density using a neural network optimized by stochastic residual minimization over a hierarchy of successively refined Nystr\"om discretizations. Upon transitioning from one level to the next, the network parameters obtained on the previous level initialize training on the current one. This coarse-to-fine strategy retains a continuous, grid-independent density representation and is designed to reduce the total computational effort required to reach a prescribed residual tolerance at the target resolution. The algorithm avoids grid-transfer operators and hierarchical fast-summation machinery, relying instead on batched kernel evaluations and standard network forward and backward passes that map efficiently onto modern GPU architectures. For uniformly stable second-kind discretizations, so strongly nonuniform contraction rates originate in the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) rather than in the discretized operator. Within each level, parameter updates can reshape the NTK, while refinement re-samples the tangent kernel on a richer discrete space and reveals directions that were not adequately resolved on coarser levels. A cross-level estimate bounds the warm-start loss in terms of the preceding training tolerance and quadrature error, motivating a tolerance schedule that balances optimization and discretization errors. Experiments on Laplace/Poisson and Helmholtz problems in two and three dimensions, together with an exterior Robin problem on a hypersurface in $\R^4$, demonstrate the method under both parametric and signed-distance surface representations at up to million-scale discretizations.
item.dc:creator: Bing-Ze Lu, Richard Tsai

item.title: Structure-Preserving Reduced-Order Modeling via Low-Rank Transport Signatures
item.description: arXiv:2607.01696v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parametrized PDEs with density-valued solutions are often difficult to approximate with classical linear reduced-order models, especially in transport-dominated regimes. We introduce an optimal-transport-based reduced-order modeling that represents each density by the Kantorovich potential transporting a fixed reference density to the target density, and then maps these potentials to transport signatures using a weighted Laplacian associated with the reference measure. This embeds the density-valued solution map in a Hilbert space while preserving control of the induced transport maps and Wasserstein error. We treat the signature map as a continuous matrix indexed by parameters and space, construct a low-rank skeleton decomposition using a maximal-volume criterion, and learn the parameter-to-coefficient map with a neural network for efficient non-intrusive online evaluation. The reconstructed solution is obtained by pushing forward the reference density, so mass and positivity preservation is built into the method. We prove a mean-squared Wasserstein error bound separating low-rank approximation, discretization, sampling, and learning errors, and demonstrate the method on density-valued continuity equation and Burgers equation, where transport signatures yield substantially lower-rank structure than the original density snapshots.
item.dc:creator: Jiajia Yu, Jingwei Hu, Fengyan Li, Shanyin Tong, Yunan Yang, Zhaiming Shen

item.title: Deep Stochastic Residual Methods for Fully Nonlinear Parabolic Equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.16730v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop and analyze neural stochastic residual methods for fully nonlinear parabolic terminal problems under exact diffusion sampling. A quadratic stochastic residual supports global training and backward regression with scalar networks and losses involving only spatial derivatives. For global training, the correction removes a Hessian penalty from the limiting first-order loss. Under a uniform output regularity budget, we bound the continuous residual norm by the square roots of the global loss or normalized backward-regression excess loss, an $O(h^{1/2})$ discretization term for time step $h$, and terminal error. Residual stability then gives value, gradient and Hessian error bounds. Under suitable solution and terminal assumptions, we construct admissible networks with $O(h^{1/2})$ bounds on these approximation errors and the square roots of both loss criteria. In ten-dimensional backward-regression tests using a shared schedule tuned for the quadratic residual, mean relative Hessian errors are $5$--$6\%$ with the quadratic residual and about $15\%$ with the first-order residual. Tuned backward regression achieves Hessian accuracy comparable to physics-informed neural networks across the tested nonlinear coefficients. Translation tests show that the ratio of Hessian error to residual can grow sharply under a fixed sampling law.
item.dc:creator: Zhenhua Zhao, Jihao Long

item.title: A stable and efficient Galerkin spectral method with asymmetrically-weighted Hermite functions for the Vlasov-Poisson system
item.description: arXiv:2608.09827v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze a Galerkin spectral method applied to the Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system based on time-independent asymmetrically-weighted (AW) Hermite functions in velocity. The VP system is written as an hyperbolic system using AW Hermite functions in velocity. Unlike the classical Petrov-Galerkin spectral method, which is not stable, the proposed Galerkin spectral method admits a natural stability in the unweighted L2 norm. This stability property enables a rigorous convergence analysis of the method. For sufficiently regular solutions with exponential decay in velocity, we establish error estimates between the exact and numerical solutions and prove convergence of the Galerkin spectral method. In particular, the method achieves spectral convergence in Sobolev spaces, with convergence rates determined by the regularity of the exact solution. Since the Gram matrix arising from the proposed Galerkin method is dense, we derive an equivalent form that retains the same approximation properties while preserving the sparsity structure similar to the classical Petrov-Galerkin method.
item.dc:creator: Ruiyang Dai

item.title: Advanced Linear Algebra with Applications - Part I (Numerical linear algebra for PDEs, machine learning, and data assimilation)
item.description: arXiv:2608.21234v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: These lecture notes form the first part of a master's-level course on advanced numerical linear algebra. Their aim is not only to present the classical algorithms, but to show why the subject has become considerably more central than it was a generation ago. Numerical linear algebra grew up alongside the numerical solution of partial differential equations, and for a long time that is where its large sparse systems came from. Ranking the nodes of a network, assimilating observations into a weather forecast, and fitting a model to a large noisy data set now lead to problems of the same kind: too large to factorise, structured, and accessible only through matrix-vector products. Strikingly few ideas are needed for all of them. Each chapter therefore develops a standard topic and then puts it to work outside its original setting. We treat norms, factorisations, conditioning and floating-point arithmetic; sparse matrices arising from finite differences, from graphs and from machine learning; stationary iterations and the smoothing property; the conjugate gradient and Lanczos methods, with spectral clustering and regularisation by early stopping; Arnoldi and GMRES, with PageRank and large least squares; and finally preconditioning, Schwarz domain decomposition and multigrid. We assume a first course in linear algebra. Every section closes with a summary of what should be retained and every chapter with exercises, several drawn from past examinations. Accompanying Python code reproduces the numerical illustrations.
item.dc:creator: Victorita Dolean, Jemima Tabeart

item.title: A simple stability analysis of the Lanczos algorithm in finite precision arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2608.21268v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a self-contained analysis of the symmetric Lanczos algorithm without reorthogonalization when computations are performed inexactly. We show the computed Lanczos vectors are well-behaved locally. From this we (i) prove Paige's loss-of-orthogonality identity, and (ii) construct a Greenbaum-type backward stability result, exhibiting a nearby problem on which exact Lanczos produces the computed tridiagonal matrix. This allows us to derive several facts about the computed Ritz values at the original eigenvalues. Our analysis simplifies the analyses of Paige and Greenbaum, at the cost of hiding polynomial factors in the iteration count.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Chen

item.title: High-order entropy-stable isothermal wall boundary condition for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.09249v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Entropy-stable boundary conditions are critical for ensuring that the corresponding numerical scheme satisfies the discrete entropy inequality, thus mimicking the second law of thermodynamics for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations discretely. Provably entropy-stable adiabatic wall boundary conditions were introduced in Parsani 2014~\cite{parsani2014entropy}. These discrete wall boundary conditions were further generalized in Dalcin 2019~\cite{dalcin2019conservative} to a moving adiabatic solid wall or a wall with a prescribed heat flux for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations discretized by using summation-by-parts (SBP) and simultaneous-approximation-term (SAT) operators. Currently, no entropy-stable formulation using SBP-SAT operators for isothermal wall boundary conditions is available in the literature. This paper presents new isothermal no-slip wall boundary conditions that: 1) enforce the $T|_{y=0}=T^{wall}$ and $\vec{v}|_{y=0}=\vec{v}^{wall}$ conditions with the design order of accuracy while maintaining stability, 2) provide the correct sign of entropy production at the wall, and 3) mimic the entropy balance of the Navier-Stokes equations at the discrete level. The structure-preserving and design-order properties of the proposed methodology are demonstrated and verified on standard benchmark problems for compressible flows.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Sayyari, Nail K. Yamaleev

item.title: A Coupled Fluid Naghdi Shell Windkessel Model for Pulmonary Artery Banding: Partitioned Numerical Scheme and Parameter Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.20966v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a 3D fluid structure interaction model for blood flow through deformable vessels with localized constrictions, motivated by pulmonary artery banding in neonates with congenital heart disease. The model couples incompressible Navier Stokes equations in an Arbitrary Lagrangian Eulerian framework with a Naghdi shell model for the arterial wall and a three element Windkessel model for downstream circulation. The shell describes a 3D cylindrical vessel wall with variable radius and is defined on a 2D reference domain. Its low regularity formulation retains membrane, bending, and transverse shear deformation while requiring only first derivatives of the reference midsurface, accommodating piecewise smooth geometries with discontinuous surface slopes. We derive the coupled variational formulation and develop a non-iterative partitioned scheme with a Robin-type interface condition incorporating arterial wall inertia. For a linearized fixed domain problem, we establish a discrete energy estimate under suitable assumptions. A unscented Kalman filter estimates proximal and distal resistances and compliance from inlet-pressure observations. Numerical experiments demonstrate consistent pressure wave propagation and wall deformation under spatial and temporal refinement. Comparisons of the standard Naghdi shell and a modified, predominantly radial shell model reveal how structural deformation mechanisms affect wave speed and displacement. An idealized pulmonary artery banding example demonstrates the coupled fluid shell Windkessel model with parameter estimation. The framework enables investigation of the hemodynamic and mechanical effects of localized constrictions and their dependence on downstream vascular properties.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Wang, Josip Tambaca, Suncica Canic

item.title: A Mixed Elliptic--Hyperbolic Monge--Amp\`ere Problem: Modeling and a Least-Squares Solver
item.description: arXiv:2610.23544v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider a transport problem motivated by freeform optical design of a parallel-to-far-field reflector. Classical formulations rely on either elliptic or hyperbolic Monge--Amp\`ere equations, leading to globally convex/concave or saddle-shape reflector geometries, respectively. However, the design of smooth reflector arrays may require optical surfaces combining both types of curvature. To address this, we introduce a mixed elliptic--hyperbolic Monge--Amp\`ere system obtained by partitioning the source domain into one elliptic and one hyperbolic subregion, and we develop a least-squares method for its numerical approximation. Numerical examples demonstrate the ability of the proposed framework to compute both isolated and periodic mixed-type transport solutions, yielding smooth reflector configurations.
item.dc:creator: G. V. Carvalho, M. J. H. Anthonissen, J. H. M. ten Thije Boonkkamp, L. Kusch, K. Mitra, W. L. IJzerman

item.title: Toward Spectral Deferred Correction Methods for Stochastic Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.23693v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The numerical solution of stochastic differential equations is computationally very demanding. Often it is of interest to evaluate certain moments, e.g., the expectation, by Monte Carlo sampling, thus requiring the computation of numerous realizations. The discretization error of the numerical scheme induces bias in the computed Monte Carlo estimator. As popular numerical schemes, like Euler-Maruyama or Milstein, are low-order, even reasonably coarse error bounds for the simulation are costly to achieve. While the evaluation of moments requires only weak convergence, in other applications like parameter estimation, strong convergence is important, but higher-order is typically harder to obtain in the strong than in the weak sense. In this paper we develop an efficient method with the potential of achieving higher strong and weak convergence order. It is based on the smooth approximation of Brownian bridges combined with spectral deferred correction methods well known for the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations. We discuss convergence, and present numerical results.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Binkowski, Matthew R. Christian, Sebastian G\"otschel, Michael L. Minion

item.title: Interacting Annealed Importance Sampling via Population-Based MCMC Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2401.15645v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling from a multimodal distribution is a fundamental and challenging problem in computational science and statistics. Among various approaches proposed for this task, one popular method is Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS). In this paper, we propose an interaction-based version of AIS by combining it with population-based Monte Carlo methods to improve its efficiency. By keeping track of an ensemble instead of a single sampler along some continuation path between the starting distribution and the target distribution, we take advantage of the interaction within the ensemble to encourage the exploration of undiscovered modes. Specifically, our main idea is to utilize either the snooker algorithm or the genetic algorithm used in Evolutionary Monte Carlo. We discuss how the proposed algorithm can be implemented and derive a partial differential equation governing the evolution of the ensemble under the continuous time and mean-field limit. We also test the efficiency of the proposed algorithm on various continuous and discrete distributions.
item.dc:creator: Haoxuan Chen, Lexing Ying

item.title: Solving Inverse Problems via Diffusion-Based Priors: An Approximation-Free Ensemble Sampling Approach
item.description: arXiv:2506.03979v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have proven to be effective in modeling high-dimensional distributions, leading to their widespread adoption for representing complex priors in Bayesian inverse problems (BIPs). However, current DM-based posterior sampling methods proposed for solving common BIPs rely on heuristic approximations to the generative process. To exploit the generative capability of DMs and avoid the usage of such approximations, we propose an ensemble-based algorithm that performs posterior sampling without the use of heuristic approximations. Our algorithm is motivated by existing work that combines DM-based methods with the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method. By examining how the prior evolves through the diffusion process encoded by the pre-trained score function, we derive a modified partial differential equation (PDE) governing the evolution of the corresponding posterior distribution. This PDE includes a modified diffusion term and a reweighting term, which can be simulated via stochastic weighted particle methods. Theoretically, we prove that the error between the true posterior and the empirical distribution of the generated samples can be bounded in terms of the training error of the pre-trained score function and the number of particles in the ensemble. Empirically, we validate our algorithm on several inverse problems in imaging to show that our method gives more accurate reconstructions compared to existing DM-based methods. Our code is available at the following Github repository~\url{https://github.com/HaoxuanSteveC00/AFDPS-TMLR}.
item.dc:creator: Haoxuan Chen, Yinuo Ren, Martin Renqiang Min, Lexing Ying, Zachary Izzo

item.title: A Level Set Method on Particle Flow Maps
item.description: arXiv:2601.09939v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate interface tracking is central to numerical simulations involving moving boundaries, including multiphase flows, free-surface dynamics, phase-change problems, and other interface-driven processes in computational mechanics. Although level set methods provide a flexible implicit representation of evolving interfaces, their grid-based advection and reinitialization procedures often introduce numerical diffusion, volume loss, and degradation of thin or highly curved structures. This paper introduces a Particle Flow Map Level Set (PFM-LS) method that addresses these limitations by transporting interface geometry through particle-carried bidirectional flow maps. In contrast to particle level set methods that use particles mainly as corrective markers, PFM-LS uses particles as primary carriers of level-set values, gradients, and Hessians within a narrow band around the interface. The method combines long-range flow-map transport, high-order particle-grid reconstruction, adaptive particle control, and a hybrid particle-grid redistancing scheme to preserve both signed-distance consistency and sub-grid geometric features. Numerical benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including topology-change tests, chamfer and Hausdorff shape-error metrics, and coupling to an incompressible free-surface flow solver, show that PFM-LS achieves strong volume preservation, high shape fidelity, and near fourth-order convergence, outperforming a broad range of existing level set and reference-map-based methods.
item.dc:creator: Jinjin He, Taiyuan Zhang, Zhiqi Li, Junwei Zhou, Duowen Chen, Bo Zhu

item.title: Rate-induced tipping in a solvable model with the Allee effect
item.description: arXiv:2601.20128v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a novel exactly solvable ordinary differential equation model for rate-induced tipping: a dynamic phenomenon of dynamical systems where a time-dependent parameter triggers the transition of stability of a system. Our model contains an Allee effect that induces a saddle point and admits an explicit solution along with the extinction threshold of a time-dependent Allee parameter. More specifically, we derive an integral inequality that serves as a necessary condition for the occurrence of rate-induced tipping. A remarkable point in the proposed model is that it can handle population extinction such that the solution completely vanishes in a finite amount of time. An unconditionally stable cubature method suitable for our model is proposed, and its superiority over the classical forward Euler method is discussed. As a proof of concept, the model reproduces the rise and fall of the membership of inland fisheries cooperatives in Japan from 1963 to 2023. The proposed model serves as a tractable tool for studying R-tipping phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Hidekazu Yoshioka

item.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2602.01176v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity (HF) simulations of parametric partial differential equations are expensive, whereas low-fidelity (LF) models such as coarse grids or simplified physics are cheap but biased. Multi-fidelity physics-informed neural networks combine the two, yet it remains unclear when cheap physics actually reduces the number of HF solves, and existing methods silently fail when the LF model is misleading and offer no guaranteed uncertainty. We answer the first question with a sharp sample-complexity bound: learning the HF field through its discrepancy from the LF model reduces the number of HF samples needed for accuracy $\varepsilon$ by the factor $\kappa^{2\gamma}$, where $\kappa$ is the ratio of the complexity of the discrepancy to that of the HF field and $\gamma$ is the effective-dimension exponent, and we confirm the predicted scaling with exact risk computations in a kernel model. Guided by the analysis, we propose GaMF-PINN, a gated multi-fidelity PINN that learns where to trust the LF model and falls back to physics-only learning where it does not, together with a function-level conformal procedure that returns uncertainty bands containing the entire HF solution with probability at least $1-\alpha$ in finite samples. We release MFPDE-Bench, an open benchmark of paired LF/HF solvers for four parametric PDEs with coarse-grid and simplified-physics LF models. Across MFPDE-Bench, GaMF-PINN reaches the accuracy of a standard HF-PINN with up to 8x fewer HF solves, remains robust when the LF model is deliberately corrupted, and attains the nominal coverage where Bayesian PINNs and deep ensembles under-cover.
item.dc:creator: laf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan, Isgandar Jafarli

item.title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
item.description: arXiv:2602.03802v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Grigory Begunov, Alexander Tyurin

item.title: Structural conditions on trust-region radius updates. Part I: first-order convergence and complexity
item.description: arXiv:2606.30202v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trust-region methods differ chiefly in how they update the radius, and each rule has traditionally been analysed on its own terms. We show that three structural conditions on the radius sequence suffice: a lower bound relative to the gradient norm, a contraction on unsuccessful iterations, and a controlled expansion on successful ones. A mechanism is weakly admissible if it satisfies the first two, and strongly admissible if it satisfies the first and third. Strong admissibility yields the optimal worst-case complexity $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ for first-order stationarity, and extends global convergence to model Hessians growing linearly with the iteration; weak admissibility gives $\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\| = 0$ under uniformly bounded model Hessians. Both hold for every rule in the class, so a new mechanism is covered by verifying two inequalities rather than by a fresh convergence proof. We verify admissibility for five mechanism classes (fixed-factor, step-driven, retrospective, criticality-anchored and gradient-scaled), prove convergence of the retrospective update under linearly growing model Hessians, and extend the Lyapunov framework of Curtis and Scheinberg (2020), Wang and Yuan (2022) to three distinct scaling factors with decoupled step acceptance, covering $\eta = 0$; its stochastic version specialises to the deterministic gradient-scaled rule. Part II treats the asymptotic behaviour of the radius and convergence to second-order critical points.
item.dc:creator: J\'er\'emy Rieussec, Fabian Bastin

item.title: Microstructure-Conditioned Surrogate Models for Graded Multiscale Optimization of Mycelium Composites
item.description: arXiv:2607.13688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Emerging sustainable materials increasingly rely on engineered hierarchy and microstructure to achieve control of their properties and mechanical behavior. Optimizing these materials with controllable microstructures requires efficient multiscale simulations. Data-driven surrogate models for the microscale can accelerate multiscale simulations, but require large amounts of data even for a fixed microstructure. When a range of microstructures is considered, as is the case in multiscale optimization, even more data is needed to train a surrogate. To overcome this challenge, we condition a hybrid physics-data surrogate on microstructural variables using a hypernetwork. This approach enables accurate predictions of multiscale mechanical behavior for a mycelium-woodchip composite material, even when trained on small datasets. The conditioned surrogate makes multiscale simulations of functionally graded structures tractable, and we validate it against a full FE^2 simulation. We optimize a graded multiscale disk, and reduce the peak stress by 43% compared to one with a random microstructure. Then, we go one step further, conditioning the network directly on manufacturing variables that can have a complex influence on the microstructure. This is a practical route to engineer the microscale for desired macroscale behavior. This contribution highlights the benefits of microarchitectured structures and demonstrates how conditioned surrogate models enable their multiscale optimization, which will accelerate the development and design of future sustainable materials and structures.
item.dc:creator: J. Storm, I. B. C. M. Rocha, S. Schyck, K. Masania, F. P. van der Meer

item.title: A counterexample to Kenig's conjecture for the Laplace double-layer operator
item.description: arXiv:2609.07947v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We disprove Kenig's 1994 spectral-radius conjecture for the double-layer operator in every dimension $d\ge2$. For every $t>1/2$ sufficiently close to $1/2$, we construct a bounded simply connected Lipschitz domain with connected boundary such that the double-layer operator on $L^2$ with respect to the surface measure has $\pm \mathrm{i} t$ in its Fredholm essential spectrum. In particular, the essential spectral radius is greater than $1/2$. In the plane, the boundary may be chosen differentiable everywhere and smooth away from a single point. Our planar construction develops a refinement mechanism that produces unbounded growth of adjoint resolvent solutions with fixed forcing while keeping the graph slopes uniformly bounded. A closed recursion for the density and its image under an auxiliary singular integral reduces the growth estimate to a certified inequality for Hermitian $2\times2$ matrices. The certificate uses continuous estimates, exact rational arithmetic and rigorous interval enclosures. Localisation and rescaled graph insertions then produce a weakly null sequence of normalised approximate eigenvectors for the adjoint double-layer operator on one bounded boundary. A compact intertwining relation on Cartesian products of the planar domain with cubes gives the higher-dimensional examples without changing the spectral parameter.
item.dc:creator: Matthew J. Colbrook, Siavash Sadeghi
